# CB RULES for the character-artist (GENERATED 2026-11-20 by tools/slice_rules.py from CB_RULES.md; do not edit)
CB_RULES.md is the master and wins. This file holds the rules that touch your job. Read it instead of the whole book. If a rule you need seems missing, grep CB_RULES.md for the word; do not read it top to bottom.

## RULE NO. 1: MAKE A RICK-QUALITY VIDEO. If this fails, everything is wrong.
(CB 2026-11-11: "no1 rule is to make ricks quality video", "if is fails everything is wrong")
- [ ] Every rule below serves this one. Following a workflow step, passing a gate or ticking a box never excuses a result that is below Rick's.
- [ ] THE TEST, on every picture and every clip before CB sees it: put ours next to a Rick frame of the same kind of shot (same shot size, same kind of place). Ask plainly: would this pass as a frame from his channel? Look at story clarity, world detail, light and shadow, reflection, colour, acting, camera.
- [ ] If ours is clearly weaker, it is NOT done. Fix it, or tell CB exactly what is still below Rick and why. Never present it as finished.
- [ ] If a workflow, tool or note leads to a result below Rick, the workflow is wrong: stop, say so, and use the method that reached the quality before (the airfield way).
- [ ] RICK'S QUALITY IS THE TARGET; TOKENS ARE A GUIDE (CB 2026-11-16: "ricks quality is the target"). The tier budget (11a2) guides how we spend; it never decides that a film may be below Rick. Never skip a check, drop a step or deliver weaker work to stay inside a budget. When reaching Rick's quality needs more than the budget, the lead says so plainly at 80 % with what it needs and why, and asks CB; the hard cap is still passed only on CB's yes.

## HARD RULE NO. 2: NOTHING GENERIC PASSES. EVERYTHING IS ULTRA DETAILED. (CB 2026-11-11: "Can we add rules hard rule. Nothing generic wont pass. Everything need to be ultra detailed")
This is a gate, not advice. A frame that fails it is not shown to CB and not rendered further.
- **Generic = fail.** A plain box, ball tree, flat one-colour surface, typed font, filler word, star in place of a word, empty prop, standing or floor-sit pose where the story needs a real action, or a set that could belong to any film.
- **Every object in frame is specific to THIS story** and built from real parts, down to the small things: a wallet has pockets, stitching, a photo and flies that fly out; a board carries a real blueprint; a cart carries the ride's name; a loop under construction shows the crane and the missing piece.
- **Scale is checked:** trees about a quarter of the hero structure, a vehicle small around its rider, characters as large in frame as Rick's.
- **Poses are specific:** seated means a chair-sit with knees forward, sleeping means slumped with a tilt; body moves come from the trained motion library.
- **The test before CB sees it:** put the frame beside Rick's and name five specific details in every main object. The five details of every prop and of the hero object are written FIRST, in `PROPS.md`, and CB OKs that list before the set build (11a step 1b, check 2). If you cannot, or if Rick's shows a kind of thing ours lacks, it fails. Fix it first.
Full detail list: section 3, "PREMIUM DETAIL IN EVERYTHING".

## 11. THE LEAN PIPELINE AND THE TOKEN RULES (CB 2026-11-15 after the armor film: "how we can optimized that is not burn too much tokes and quicker to make", "or what takes so much time and not worth", then "yes please do."). Wins over every older pipeline line in this file and in SKILL.md.
Why: the armor film (63.5 s) cost 1.66 billion tokens, 41 helpers and 22.7 working hours. Measured: about 750 million went into a still-picture storyboard with judge rounds that CB rejected when he saw it move; 97 % of all tokens were re-reading (every step a helper takes re-reads everything it has seen so far); builder 1 alone cost 184 million because one conversation ran 13 hours. Target for the next film of the same quality: at most 450 million tokens and 12 working hours. Since 2026-11-16 the budget comes from the film's QUALITY TIER (11a2), per finished minute.

### 11a. The lean pipeline (the order of work)
0. THE LEAN WAY IS THE DEFAULT FROM THE NEXT FILM (CB 2026-11-17, after the two lean test rounds: "its improve alot and also safe tokes.", then "Yes, apply the rule changes" on the card "Make the lean way the default for new films now?" and "yes" in the thread). Proof and numbers: `episodes/_tests/lean_2026-11-17/` (REPORT.md, r2/REPORT_r2.md, RULE_CHANGES_PROPOSAL.md). Where a step below names separate board, build-out, camera-director and fix-round helpers for one stretch, this paragraph wins:
   - ONE BUILDER PER STRETCH does the board, the build-out AND the camera, in one session. The camera plan (stations, holds; no "travel" overrides unless a whip) is LOCKED and passes `python tools/film_plan.py check` (with its window speed check, `--window a-b`) BEFORE the first render. Fix rounds stay inside the same builder while its time box lasts (11b T9b); after the time box a fresh builder continues from STATE.md (11b T2). Measured: lean r1 + r2 = 1 builder, 0 helpers, 0 cuts, camera p90 18.2 px/f against 21.8 for the old pipeline.
   - KIT REUSE FIRST: sets, cast, props, moves, bike and vehicle fits, grade and captions from the earlier films before anything new is built. Hard Rule No. 2 stays: every reused object gets FIVE story-specific details (lettering, wear, place marks, period parts, props) before it counts as done (ESTIMATE: not measured in the test; the reused traffic-lights kit already had them).
   - DEPARTMENT AGENTS ONLY FOR NEW KIT: set-builder, character-artist, props-hero, animator and the camera-director are called when the stretch needs a NEW set, person, prop, move, or a camera idea the builder cannot find in the move library (11h), not by default.
   - ONE COMMAND PER STRETCH CYCLE: `bash tools/run_stretch.sh <film.json> <a-b>` (bake, plan check with the window speed check, GPU render, frame checks with the driver and body rows, 11i detail gate, cam_track numbers, one log).
1. STORY AND VOICE, THEN THE PICTURE PLAN. One story unless CB asks for a choice; facts checked; voice recorded; `words.json`; then `PICTURE_PLAN.md` (11d): what the viewer sees on each word, written for this story.
1b. THE FIVE PRE-BUILD CHECKS (CB 2026-11-16: "ok add this to the worklow", approving the coordinator's list of five steps "that make the quality before the build, not after"). Why: the last films went over budget and needed extra rounds because the faults were found after the gate (traffic lights: the car rebuilt after the gate, every stretch rendered twice for the camera; braking lines: the world at half Rick's detail found on v7; armor: the stills passed what the moving film failed). Each check is cheap and catches one of those before anything is built. Steps 2 and 3 are QUICK OKs in the chat (CB says yes or strikes a line), never a polish round; THE ONE GATE (step 2) stays the only review gate. They come out of the tier budget (11a2); the budget itself does not change.
   1. REFERENCE PACK, BEFORE THE SCRIPT IS LOCKED. The `rick-researcher` picks 5-10 Rick frames PER BEAT from `references/` (same job in the story, same shot size, same kind of place, same light), writes `episodes/<name>/refs/REF_PACK.md` (beat, frame file, what to take: camera, staging, light, detail) and one small sheet per beat. It PICKS from the studies we have; it does not study Rick again (11b T8). The writer locks the script only when every beat has its frames. Every later side-by-side (checks 3-5, Rule No. 1) uses these frames, so no helper hunts for a reference again. Frames stay private.
   2. HERO OBJECT MODEL AND PROP LIST, CB OKs BEFORE THE SET BUILD. After the picture plan, the `props-hero` builds the hero object model (three views, in its character's fist, beside the Rick frame of the same kind of object) and writes `episodes/<name>/PROPS.md`: every prop the plan names, who holds it, its real size, its era, and FIVE SPECIFIC DETAILS for this story (Hard Rule No. 2). The lead posts the hero sheet and the list in the chat; CB says yes or strikes a line. No set or prop is built before that yes.
   3. ONE-PAGE LOOK CARD, CB OKs IT. Before any set is built, the lead makes `episodes/<name>/LOOK_CARD.jpg` (one page, phone readable): the colour world (12c: its name, 3-5 hex, the one accent), the key light direction and the time of day per place, the period and place, each beside 1-2 Rick frames of the same light from the reference pack. It is the summary of LOOK_BIBLE.md (11c), not a new document. CB says yes or changes a line in the chat; the look pack (11c) is built from it.
   4. HOOK TEST FIRST. Before the rest of the film is built, the hook builder builds frame 0 and the first 10-15 s AT FULL DETAIL (look pack, dressing at the 11i gate, light, the acted gag, voice and captions) from the hook stretch's camera plan (2b). The lead puts it beside the hook frames of the reference pack (one sheet and one side-by-side clip at full speed). If ours is not clearly as strong as Rick's (Rule No. 1: frame 0 as the hook picture, story readable with the sound off, world detail, light, camera), STOP there: fix the method on the hook and test again; never start the other stretches on a method that loses. When it passes, the hook clip goes to CB in the chat at once (to see, not a gate; CB's yes at the one gate covers it) and the other stretches start.
   5. CHECKS AFTER EVERY SCENE, NOT ONLY AT THE END. Each scene (each stretch render, board and polish alike) runs in its run.sh, in the same call: `node tools/frame_checks/check.mjs`, `node tools/camsafe/validate.mjs` and a Rick side-by-side sheet (ours beside its beat's reference pack frames, small, 11b T3). A FAIL or a weaker-than-Rick sheet stops that scene and is fixed before the builder reports; the other scenes go on. The final still gets the full run (section 7).
2. THE ONE GATE: THE WHOLE FILM ROUGH, PLUS THE HOOK MOVING. As soon as the hook test passes (1b, check 4), one builder per remaining stretch starts at once (section 10) with a cap of 60-90 minutes and brings 2-3 real three.js key frames for EVERY line of its stretch: no polish, stand-in cast allowed. The hook is the 10-15 s of the hook test (1b, check 4), at full detail, with voice and captions. CB sees the picture plan, the whole board with its line check (every scene already through its checks, 1b check 5) and the moving hook together, and says yes or no. Nothing but the hook is polished and no judge runs before this gate. Why both: the armor film showed that stills cannot prove motion or camera (CB rejected what the stills had passed); the Moonrakers film showed that polishing one scene for a day before CB has seen the whole film wastes the day (CB 2026-11-14: "til now i dint see the storybaord", then "Board all 20 lines now"). This replaces the hook-frame gate of section 0.
2b. THE CAMERA PLAN, BEFORE ANY STRETCH RENDERS IN MOTION (CB 2026-11-16 after elevator, Monopoly, braking lines and fake surgery all came out with a fast, jumpy camera: "previousd work didnt have this issue now the issue is back. you need to know before this happen. so avoid it"; "you can not make one mesurement as norm since every episode is different"). Why it came back: the old stage 5 (camera-director + `film_plan.py check`) had no place in this lean list, so the stretch builders put one camera station on every picture-plan row (about 80 in 74 s), and "one flying take" (11f) turned the cuts between them into whips. The films before the lean pipeline (lightning spear, goldrush) had the camera step and did not have the fault. Rule:
   - A PICTURE-PLAN ROW IS NOT A CAMERA STATION. Rows say what the viewer must see on a word; one camera move flows through several rows (follow the thing that moves, push in, rise up the tall thing, cross the set).
   - The `camera-director` writes each stretch's camera from the built sets BEFORE its builder renders motion: one flowing idea per place, with the reason for every move from this scene, written in the stretch's CAMERA_NOTE.md.
   - The scene decides the numbers, not one norm: `python tools/film_plan.py check` runs in every stretch's run.sh before any render and prints the camera bands as a WARNING list. A camera band may be outside only with this scene's reason in CAMERA_NOTE.md. A station teleport (a jump in one frame inside a take) and an unplanned whip are always FAIL.
   - CAMERA V2 ON EVERY NEW FILM (CB 2026-11-16 "Yes, fix and re-test"; proof reel episodes/_tests/camera_rules_2026-11-16/CAMERA_TEST_V2.md, CINEMATOGRAPHY.md section 7). Every new film.json starts with `"camera": {"v2": true}`: travel time grows with distance (1.5 s + 0.25 s/m, up to 6 s), speed is checked against the subject, stations too close are flowed through (WARN), close rests keep drifting, `whip: true` is a capped 9-frame whip, eases are timed on picture speed. Measured on the 12-move test: parked 25 % -> about 1 %, near-to-far peak 33 -> 19, the builders' 1-station-per-second hop -> one flowing move. Films already rendering without the switch stay as they are (without it the bake is byte-identical to before). Every camera v2 WARN is read and fixed or given its scene reason in CAMERA_NOTE.md.
   - THE COMPARISON BEFORE THE REST RENDERS: the lead measures the first moving stretch with tools/measure/cam_track.py and watches it at full speed beside a Rick clip of the same kind of scene (references/reports/CAMERA_TEST_ALL_2026-11-16.md: our approved lightning spear parks as much as the faulty films, so it is not the model) before the other stretches render. If ours moves faster, hops more or feels less controlled, stop and fix the plan; never render four more stretches on it.
3. BUILD OUT AND POLISH THE STRETCHES from the approved board, in parallel (section 10), from ONE shared sets folder from the first day (never a copy of the sets per stretch), with the strong colours already in (11c). CB's approved board is the FLOOR: a polished frame keeps every story element its board panel shows (props, characters, the gag, the named thing) and the light of its chapter; the builder checks board beside polish before reporting, and every scene runs its checks as it renders (1b, check 5).
4. CB'S NOTES IN BATCHES. The lead collects all notes on a version, runs the automatic checks first, then sends ONE fix round per version. Aim: two rounds.
5. SOUND, then THE GRADE as the last picture step, then delivery.
ONE FOLDER PER FILM (CB 2026-11-15: "never create so many subfolder. for one keep same name and create inside subfolder with version"). A film lives in ONE folder, `episodes/<name>/`, named after the film, never after a prompt or a task. Stretches, versions, fixes and tests go INSIDE it: `episodes/<name>/s2/`, `episodes/<name>/v3/`, `episodes/<name>/_tmp/`. Never a sibling folder such as `<name>-s2`, `<name>-s4a-raid`, `_ridefix_tmp_s4a` or `continue-<name>-from-handoff...`. Every helper brief names its subfolder inside the film folder. Temp folders are deleted when their stretch lands. At delivery the film folder keeps the final video, the scripts, the notes and the code; frame folders, old versions and logs are deleted. DELETE DIRECTLY, WITHOUT ASKING, as soon as the final is approved (CB 2026-11-15: "next time please delete directly after everything final keep only neccessary files and final files"): keep the final video(s), scripts, notes, code, cast, refs, sets and sound; delete every frame folder, old version, old animatic, log and temp folder. Then decode the kept final once to prove it plays.
TAKEN OUT FOR NOW (CB 2026-11-16, after seeing the cost table of the armor film: "ok lets take it out for now. update the skill"). These are not done at all, not even as a test, until CB asks for one of them by name in a new message:
- LIGHT ROUNDS ON THE STORYBOARD (day light, glints, shadows, lantern glow worked on still pictures by the lighting-director): 159 million tokens and about 4 hours on the armor film, rebuilt for the moving film anyway. Light now comes from the LOOK_BIBLE colour targets and light colours per place written BEFORE the sets are built (11c), and the stretch builders set it in their own takes. The lighting-director is called only to write those targets.
- EFFECTS ROUNDS ON THE STORYBOARD (dust puffs, light beams through holes, glow passes worked on still pictures by the vfx-artist): 104 million tokens and about 3 hours, same reason. Effects now come only from the "effect or gag" column of the picture plan (11d) and are built by the stretch builder inside its take, from `templates/pieces/` where a piece fits. The vfx-artist is called only for one effect the picture plan names that no piece covers, inside a stretch, on the moving clip.
- THE BLENDER LAYER (shiny metal, glass, materials, the RunPod Blender render): 76 million tokens and about 6 hours plus RunPod for a gain that is hard to see on a phone. No Blender pass of any kind, also not for a shiny hero object, until CB asks. The look-finisher and 3d-designer are not called. `episodes/armor-no-holes/blender_metal/RUNPOD.md` and `rules/parked/BLENDER_PARKED.md` (every Blender rule taken out of this file on 2026-11-16) are the record of how to do it when CB asks.
A STEP TAKEN OUT KEEPS ITS GUARD (CB 2026-11-16, same note). Before a step is taken out of the pipeline, or a rule changes how the camera, the cast or the cut works, the lead writes in one line what that step protected and which remaining step now protects it (a check in run.sh, a brief line, a helper). No guard named, no change. Check this list when a fault CB once fixed comes back: the camera fault of 2026-11-16 came back because "department rounds on still pictures" were taken out and the camera plan went with them.
Also not in the pipeline any more:
- Department rounds on still pictures BEFORE the gate (camera, light, props and effects each sending fix rounds on a storyboard) and judge loops. On the armor film three such rounds chased judge scores of 5.5 and 6.8 and none of that work reached the film; on Moonrakers six judge and fix rounds went into 7.5 s while 18 lines were not started. A judge runs at most ONCE per version, AFTER the gate, on the moving clip and its sheets; never judge, fix, judge more than twice without CB seeing the version. The lead still LOOKS at the check sheets before CB sees anything (section 7 stays).
- A repaint of finished sets. Colour is decided before the sets are built (11c).

### 11b. Token rules (every helper and the lead)
- T1 READ ONLY YOUR SLICE. A helper reads `rules/dept/<its department>.md` (made by `python tools/slice_rules.py`) and the files its brief names. It never reads the whole of CB_RULES.md or SKILL.md; when it needs one more rule it greps for the word. Only the lead reads the whole book, once per session. LEAN DEFAULT (2026-11-17): the stretch builder too reads only its slice (its rows of the picture plan, the guards of 11a2, the 11h camera moves, 11i), never all of CB_RULES, SKILL and HANDOFF at its first step (measured: lean r1 carried about 100 k tokens of that first read through every later step).
- T2 A FRESH HELPER FOR EVERY FIX ROUND. A helper does one build or one fix round, then it ends. Before it reports it writes `STATE.md` in its work folder (at most 60 lines): what is built, the files and frame folders, the numbers measured, what is weak, what is open. The next round is a NEW helper that reads STATE.md and the notes. Never resume a helper that already did a round: each resumed step re-reads its whole history. LEAN DEFAULT (2026-11-17): the one stretch builder of 11a step 0 does its own fix rounds while its time box lasts (T9b); this rule applies when the time box ends. (This replaces "one builder who stays through every fix round" in section 10.)
- T3 NUMBERS BEFORE PICTURES. Anything a script can measure is checked by a script that prints numbers: a figure cut by the frame edge, the named thing in frame on its word, floor share, saturation and brightness, frozen frames, loudness. A helper opens a picture only when a number fails or for the one final look. Pictures are looked at small: one sheet at most 1,600 px wide, at most 4 pictures per check round, never full-size frames one by one.
- T4 ONE COMMAND PER CYCLE. Render, sheets and measurements run from ONE script call. A long run goes in the background and the helper ends its turn; it does not wake up to wait, poll or look at a log. Every wake-up re-reads everything.
- T5 SHORT REPORTS, DETAIL IN FILES. A helper's report is at most 25 lines: done, numbers, weak points, files. Tables and lists go into a file the report names.
- T6 THE SMALL MODEL FOR MECHANICAL WORK. Rendering, joining, measuring, merging, fact checks, sound mix runs and file moves go to a helper on the smaller model (Agent tool `model: sonnet` or `haiku`). The main model is for story, acting, camera and look decisions. LEAN DEFAULT (2026-11-17): no helper by default. A stretch builder starts at most ONE small-model helper, and only for render and measure (no judging, no building), with its own time box (ESTIMATE: render and measure are about 10-15 % of a stretch's tokens).
- T7 A FRESH LEAD SESSION PER PHASE. Story, build and finish are three sessions, each started from HANDOFF.md. The lead never reads a helper's transcript and never pastes long tool output into the chat when a file path will do.
- T8 NOTHING BUILT TWICE. Before a helper builds a tool, a set part or a move, it greps `tools/`, `templates/` and the last episode for one that exists. Studies of Rick are done once and live in the rules and `references/`; a film does not study him again unless CB names a new question. Also before a new check or rig: grep `tools/` and `templates/` for one made the same day (lean r2 wrote scale_check.mjs while body_check.mjs was being written in another thread).
- T9 MEASURE EVERY FILM. At delivery the lead runs `python tools/token_report.py` and writes the totals into HANDOFF.md: tokens per helper, working hours, and the three most expensive helpers with the reason. A helper over 60 million tokens is a fault to explain.
- T9b TIME BOX PER BUILDER AND PER HELPER (lean default, 2026-11-17): about 60 steps per 7 s stretch window; when it ends the builder writes STATE.md and stops. Measured: lean r1 65 steps 16.9 M tokens, r2 72 steps about 15 M (with four extra CB notes and a new check tool). EXPECTED TOKENS with a reused kit: about 2-4 M per film second (measured: r1 2.4 M/s; r1 + r2 together about 4.6 M/s), so about 150-250 M for a 60 s film when the kit exists (ESTIMATE), against 720 M measured for traffic lights; a film that needs new sets and cast costs more (ESTIMATE: +100-200 M). The quality tiers (11a2) stay the budget cap; these are the expected spend inside them.

## 12. THE CREATIVE EDGE: MATCH RICK ON CAMERA AND WORLD, BEAT HIM ON CHARACTER ACTING (CB 2026-11-16: "ok add it", approving the suggestion "we match Rick on camera and world and beat him on character acting"; with "i want something creative agent to add that thinks more out of the box")
Why: Rule No. 1 makes Rick the floor, and a floor alone makes a copy. The old study law of the skill already asked for a CREATIVITY GAP (every idea we take from him carries one invention of our own; every film has something his films have no equivalent of), but no step of the pipeline produced it. We keep his pacing, script pattern, camera moves and world density (sections 1, 6, 11e-11h) and win where his films are thin: his characters mostly stand, point and react with one face.
- [ ] 12a CHARACTERS THAT PERFORM. Every beat gets ONE small acted gag on its word: a double take, a fumble and catch, a proud pose that backfires, a too-careful tiptoe, a slow glance to the lens, a held breath that ends in a cough. It is built from the acting faces (char2d FACES: think, concentrate, aim, lipBite, holdBreath, browUp, nervousSmile, glanceCam, proud), the grips and the funny movement library (`pick({ action, feeling, energy, persona })`), written as an ACTING SEQUENCE with times (section 5, CHARACTER ACTING) and played by the animator as an episode move. It reads with the sound off. It keeps the older limits: one action or one feeling per beat (section 9), never over key narration, the face calm first and changing on the word, dead still once settled, the cast's own personality (CAST_PERSONALITY.md). No two beats of one film use the same gag mechanism.
- [ ] 12b ONE SIGNATURE SHOT PER FILM. One picture Rick would never make, built around THIS story's hero object: ride inside it, the set transforms in one move (the cell folds out of the board, the bell turns into the stage), the object at a scale or from an angle only this story allows. It sits on the TURN or the CLIMAX row, is entered and left by a camera move (never a hard cut), and still passes the camera-safe, frame and grounding checks; kid-safe. It may also be the film's impossible view (11f), but it must be ours: never a shot from a Rick film. It is proven first, alone, like a hero object (Ultra: its own helper, 11a2; Standard and Premium: the first thing its stretch builder proves).
- [ ] 12c A COLOUR WORLD PER FILM. Each film has its own bold palette, written in LOOK_BIBLE.md before any set is built (11c): a plain name ("tin-toy red and pool-table green"), 3-5 key colours as hex, the ONE loud accent on the hero object, ONE SIGNATURE COLOUR ON THE HERO ONLY (CB 2026-11-17: "what you can learn fromhere to make our video better", then "yes can add all"; source: the "Miner Who Fed Ghosts" prompt, project files rules/miner_prompt_2026-11-17.md: the old miner's red neckerchief is the only red on any person): the hero character wears one signature colour that no other person in the film wears, checked on the cast sheet (in a one-red film this is usually the red), and how the palette SHIFTS with the mood of the story (start, turn, low point, payoff), riding on the light kinds the plan already has. It keeps the 11c numbers (saturation, night brightness at least 0.31, one red, faces white by day), Rick's natural grass and sky unless the story's world is not natural (a toy, a board game, a dream), and it is never the palette of the last film. It goes on the LOOK CARD that CB OKs before the sets (11a step 1b, check 3).
- [ ] 12d WHO MAKES IT. The `creative-director` agent (agents/creative-director.md, slice rules/dept/creative-director.md) runs ONCE per film, right after the script and voice and before the picture plan is final. It writes `episodes/<name>/CREATIVE.md`: one acted gag per beat with its mechanism, three signature-shot ideas with one picked and why, the colour world, and up to five more fresh ideas (a running gag, a set that tells a joke, a transition through the hero object, a sound idea, a title idea). It reads only the script, words.json, CAST_PERSONALITY.md and its slice; it never builds and never re-studies Rick (11b T8). The writer and the lead take what fits into PICTURE_PLAN.md (columns "acted gag" and "signature"); CB sees CREATIVE.md with the picture plan at the one gate and can strike any idea. Cost: about 1-3 M tokens.
- [ ] 12e THE GUARD. The creative edge never overrides a CB rule: Rule No. 1 (each picture beside a Rick frame of the same kind of shot; weaker = not done), Hard Rule No. 2, the locked cast and views, the camera rules, the facts of the story. Never copy Rick's story, characters, gags or shots; his frames stay private. Every tier (11a2) carries it: Standard = the gags and the colour world, the signature shot reusing kit parts; Premium and Ultra build the signature shot new.

## 4. Characters
- [ ] FACES (ONE RULE; merges seven older face lines of 2026-11-11 to 2026-11-15, newest wins; CB 2026-11-13 night: "No shade on faces. keep the drawn shade that make 3d look. but no shade from hair or hat or anything else on face."; CB 2026-11-15: "dont delete this premade face shadow. the wone that generate shadow on face only", "why keep making the same mistake? the shadow on his face"):
  - THE DRAWN SHADE STAYS: the template's own thin soft crescent on the side away from the light (char2d faceShadow; film.json face_shadow true or unset) is the ONLY shade on a face. Never stack a second head shadow on it (edge_shadow.py is not used on v12+ cards).
  - NOTHING ELSE SHADES A FACE: no hat, brim or hair shadow, no costume shade on skin, no shadow from a prop, an arm, a table or another character, no coloured light rim, no card or scene light that darkens it in patches. Kit settings on every film: `card_shade.amount` 0 AND `card_shade.rim_amount` 0, no `far` colour light on the cast, `card_shade.hat_shadow` 0 (default since 2026-11-12), `costume_shade.keep_drawn_light: true` (keeps every white and light-grey drawn pixel, also white animals), `costume_shade.smooth: 40` (no horizontal streaks in hair beside the face; the hair library's own curls and strands stay).
  - WHITE BY DAY, TINT ONLY: the face reads white in a day scene. It may take the COLOUR of the scene light (pink-white in a pink cell, cool white at night, warm white at sunset), never a darker patch; the warm light of a place is shown on the costume, the props and the set. This replaces the 2026-11-11 "self lit" lock and the 22:16 "face goes darker at night" line.
  - CHECK: the face-and-hair zoom on the first frame of every new character and on every sheet: a grey patch or band on a face that the template did not draw = fix before sending.

- [ ] CHARACTER PRESETS, PRESERVE IDENTITY, VARY PERFORMANCE (CB 2026-11-13 02:27-02:28 Bangkok: "Build a unified Character ID system... When a scene calls CHAR_002, automatically load or reconstruct the exact registered character... Do not generate a new interpretation from text", and "Every character must be generated from a rule-locked preset. Preserve the approved visual identity exactly, including silhouette, proportions, face design, outfit, colors, and style language. Only vary pose, expression, camera angle, and animation performance within the allowed preset rules."). Every character in every film is called by its ID (CHAR_001...) and built from its saved preset, never redrawn from a text description. A preset has 5 sections: 1 CHARACTER ID (id, name, style family); 2 VISUAL BLUEPRINT = the LOCKED layer (head shape, face layout, eye and mouth design, hair, beard, face fill, body size from the three-size bible, limb style, outfit key and colours from the 500-outfit library, approved costume variants, accessories, silhouette, line style, art style), linked to the exact master asset: castkit spec + bible_sizes entry for the 2D puppet, its golden sheet PNGs per view, and the Blender/GLB card when there is one; 3 PERSONALITY AND ACTING BLUEPRINT (the CAST_PERSONALITY profile: temperament, acting style, micro-behaviours, signature gestures, reaction speed, relationships); 4 ALLOWED VARIATIONS = the PERFORMANCE layer (expression from our face set, lip-sync mouths, arm and leg pose from the motion library, body rotation within the four locked views, action, emotion, camera angle, scene-light response, prop grips); 5 FORBIDDEN DEVIATIONS (never change head shape, hair or hair colour, face design, outfit silhouette or colours, limb style, size, line style or art style; no random accessories; no new outfit unless it is an approved variant). Hardest locked, almost 100 %: head shape, face layout, hair, outfit silhouette, main colours, body proportions, art style. PRESET COMPLIANCE CHECK before any shot goes on: silhouette, colours, head shape, face design, outfit, proportions, line style match the preset sheet in every view; the personality reads; only allowed variations changed. If not, revise before approving. Films already in animation keep their cast, now registered as presets. HOW WE RUN IT: the master registry (character bible) lives in the kit with the bible and outfit library and is built in the thread "Build Character ID system"; the character-artist owns the presets and runs the compliance check, the writer names IDs in the shot table, and the storyboard-judge fails any frame where a character drifts from its preset.

For the locked cast it is a detail the approved drawing ALREADY has, written into the preset, never a redraw; a NEW character gets one designed in and shown on its preset sheet before CB locks it. The PRESET COMPLIANCE CHECK looks for it in every view used; missing or moved = drift.

The face takes the light's COLOUR only, as FACES says. Check on the first look frame: character beside the set, does it look lit by that world?

### 11d2. CAMERA CONTINUITY AND CONTACT CHECKS (CB 2026-11-16, pasted "UNIVERSAL HUMAN-LIKE ANIMATION, PHYSICAL INTERACTION & CAMERA CONTINUITY SYSTEM", then "ok"). The body-mechanics half of that text was already here (section 5, BODY MECHANICS, CONTACT AND GROUNDING); these are the parts that were new.
- ONE WORLD, THE CAMERA ONLY LOOKS AT IT. A pure camera move never turns, moves or re-poses a character. Every act gives the character a direction in the world with "look" (a cast name, a world point [x, y, z] or "cam"); `tools/film_plan.py` (apply_looks, since 2026-11-10) then picks front / 3/4 / side / back and the screen direction from where the lens stands on every frame. "look_full": true = the true angle (camera behind him shows his back); without it the view is cheated open to the lens as Rick does. Never set "view" by hand for a shot where the camera goes around a character.
- THE SAME MOMENT FROM TWO ANGLES (CB's example): he sits on the chair holding a cup. Shot A front: hips on the seat, feet on the floor, cup in his right hand. Shot B from the side: the same seat contact and the same grip. Shot C over the shoulder: chair, cup, hands, body direction and room exactly where they were. He does not turn to the camera unless the story makes him.
- Moves: most library moves have a side and a front drawing only. When the camera needs his 3/4 or back during a move, the stretch builder checks that the move has that view or builds it; a move shown in the wrong view is a fault.
- CHECKS (numbers before pictures, 11b T3):
  - `python tools/film_plan.py check` gate "camera goes around a figure but its view never changes": FAIL when the camera goes 45 deg or more around a figure that stays in place and on screen while its view stays the same (found in Monopoly s2 and s4).
  - `node tools/frame_checks/check.mjs` adds four rows: seat (a sitting figure's hips ON the seat: more than 6 cm above it = FAIL, no seat under the hips = FAIL), overlap (two figures within 35 cm in the world and 25 % or more overlapping on screen = inside each other), slide (a planted foot of the move sliding across the picture: over 3 cm per frame = FAIL, over 1.2 = WARN; travel toward or away from the lens is not counted), prop_in_hand (a held 3D prop whose fist the arm does not reach). Tiny far figures (under 12 % of the frame height) give WARN instead of FAIL.
  - Proof (2026-11-16): a customer lifted 30 cm off her chair = seat FAIL 32 cm; two printers placed 10 cm apart = overlap FAIL 99 %; the approved Goldrush s7 diners all PASS on their chairs. The slide check finds the library runs in Goldrush s1 and s3 sliding 1.3-23 cm per frame (the hand-locked hook runners pass).
- A FAULT IS FIXED IN THE MOVE, THE RIG OR THE ACT, never hidden by the camera framing.
- [ ] CAMERA-SAFE CHARACTERS (CB 2026-11-16 12:31Z, decision card in the thread "Build camera-safe 2.5D character rig": the camera-safe rig is the default for new films). New films set film.json "camsafe": true (back and 3/4 views for library moves, true seated views, seat tip and depth nudge under high cameras; old films stay as they are, pixel-identical). Before CB sees any version run `node tools/camsafe/validate.mjs <film.json>` next to frame_checks; any FAIL (RIG_ERROR, VIEW_MISMATCH, FACE_BEHIND, LEGS_DISAGREE, SEAT_DRIFT, STEEP, LOW, FACE_HIDDEN, FLICKER, MEME_SIDE) is fixed first, with the least disruptive fix: move the camera a few degrees, then switch or add a drawing, then change the act. Never turn or squash a card toward the lens; cards already face and tip to it (VIEW RULE 1). Details: tools/camsafe/README.md.

## RULES FROM OTHER SECTIONS THAT NAME YOUR SUBJECT
### from 0. How to work (before anything is built)
- [ ] OPTIMIZE FIRST (CB 2026-11-13 20:5x Bangkok, bomber armor thread: "anything that help us to optimized and make it better is always first rule"). Whenever a film shows a way to make the pipeline faster or the result better, that improvement goes into the rules and the tools FIRST, in the same turn, before the next step of the film. Say plainly what went wrong, why, and what changes.
- [ ] Show CB everything in the chat. No steps for CB at the PC. Only the final film is saved on the PC (and copied to OneDrive).
- [ ] Need CB's OK: any online/RunPod render, changes to the locked cast or MAIN LOOK. One Blender job at a time.



### from 2. Every picture (the mechanism)
- [ ] FRAME 0 IS THE HOOK: a character doing the strange act with the hero object readable. Never an object close-up, at the start or as the loop frame. ("start frame should be something noticeable, a hook")
- [ ] EXACT WORDS AND ONE ACTION ON A NAMED WORD, EVERY BEAT (CB 2026-11-17: "what you can learn fromhere to make our video better", then "yes can add all"; source: the "Miner Who Fed Ghosts" prompt, project files rules/miner_prompt_2026-11-17.md). Every beat of the picture plan quotes the narration word for word from `voice/words.json` (never a summary), with its start second, and names ONE action that lands on ONE named word of it (on "knock" two taps come from the dark; "Tap. Creak. Tap." = one action on each word). A beat whose words are paraphrased or whose action floats free of a word is not a plan row.
- [ ] ONE PLANNED STILLNESS PER FILM (CB 2026-11-17: "what you can learn fromhere to make our video better", then "yes can add all"; source: the "Miner Who Fed Ghosts" prompt, project files rules/miner_prompt_2026-11-17.md). Every shot has something moving: a character, a prop, the light, the air (dust, drips, smoke) or the camera. The film may have ONE planned stillness, where the story itself stops (a question, the beat after a disaster): everything freezes on purpose, marked STILLNESS in the plan with its reason. Any other shot where nothing moves is a fault. The stillness is the only exception to "the camera never stops" (6, 11h M00).
- [ ] DEPTH IN EVERY SHOT (CB 2026-11-17: "what you can learn fromhere to make our video better", then "yes can add all"; source: the "Miner Who Fed Ghosts" prompt, project files rules/miner_prompt_2026-11-17.md): three layers, each from this set: a REAL, RECOGNISABLE prop close to the lens (a candle, a lunch tin, a beam, a pick handle; soft in focus but you can tell what it is), the characters, and a world that goes on far behind them. Never a grey or blurry blob near the lens, never an empty back wall. The near prop never sits between the lens and a face (11i). The plan names the near prop and the far world per row.
- [ ] Literal sense: the picture must make sense for the line and the place. ("why standing sleeping that not make sense")
- [ ] Stay in the story's world: analogy scenes use the same period, place and cast. No modern set in a period story.

### from 3. World and look (Rick's 3D world, never a flat drawing)
- [ ] The WORLD is real 3D with real materials, light, shadow and reflection. Only the characters are flat 2D cards. A flat 2D drawing of the whole scene is wrong. ("oh no. what are you doing that is not like ricks")
- [ ] One strong key light you can see or infer (sun, window, lamp). Hard long shadows of characters and props; shaped light patches (window bars); colour bounce from strong colours; lamps glow. Light shafts only on the hook or a dramatic beat, soft and see-through. (Pink Prison)
- [ ] No ink lines on the world; ink only on characters. No film grain.
- [ ] Background blur: wides and mediums fully sharp; only close-ups get a mild soft background. Characters NEVER blur. ("background blur is too much", "characters never blur. always sharp")
- [ ] RICK FINISH (CB 2026-11-11: "apply everything that makes it more to rick clips style"; measured on his roller coaster film against ours, report https://claude.ai/artifact/H62bCh9DCKS58eqqD4vDVM):
  - Every character and prop throws a hard shadow on the ground from the one key light. No grey blob under the feet.
  - CONTACT SHADOW (ambient occlusion) where feet and things meet the ground (CB 2026-11-11: "do we have ambient occlusion?", "is like the shadow at the foot of character and ground"): a small, soft, DARK patch right under each sole and under every prop, crate, stall leg and wheel, tight to the contact (about the width of the foot, fading within a few cm), on top of the long hard cast shadow, never instead of it, and never a big grey oval. Also soft darkening in corners, under overhangs and where walls meet the floor. (Blender how-to: parked file.) Check on every look frame: zoom on the feet, the character must look planted, not pasted on.
  - Surfaces carry real detail: wood grain and separate planks, corrugated metal, brick by brick, carpet nap, grass as blades with light and dark patches, dirt with pebbles. His fine surface detail measures 2 to 4 times a flat-colour set. No flat single-colour surfaces in a finished frame.
  - Hero objects are real models (BlenderKit first), not blocks: a car has a windscreen, bumper, chrome and wheels; a stump has bark and roots; stalls have goods.
  - Shiny highlights on chrome, paint, glass and lamps (about 1-2 % of the frame), and dark accents in the shadows; haze lifts the darkest 1 % to about 0.08-0.15 (measured on 25 of his films 2026-11-11, section 6b).
  - Depth: something big and close in the frame (a beam, a post, the edge of a cart), a pale far distance, corners a little darker.
  - Night is deep blue moonlight with small white-hot bulbs and ONE warm lamp pool. Never purple or orange ground, no oversized coloured bulbs.
  - Characters large in frame, hands doing the exact thing (wallet open in both hands, grip on the hammer handle).
  - Effects are real light and smoke (fire, sparks, glow streaks), not flat cut-out shapes.
- [ ] EVERY LIGHT HAS A VISIBLE SOURCE, AND THE LIGHT FOLLOWS THE STORY (CB 2026-11-17: "what you can learn fromhere to make our video better", then "yes can add all"; source: the "Miner Who Fed Ghosts" prompt, project files rules/miner_prompt_2026-11-17.md). Each light in a shot comes from a source the viewer sees or feels: a candle on a hat, a window, a lamp, a screen, the low sun behind a building, a shaft of daylight. No light from nowhere. The light of a place CHANGES with the story beats, written per beat in LOOK_BIBLE.md and on the LOOK CARD: e.g. warm and safe at the start, colder and bluer when the trouble starts, the bright exit becoming the key light the characters run toward, the brightest frame at the payoff. Faces take the scene light: a warm side and a cool side, never flat or grey (section 4 FACES). (Its Blender half, "Blender keeps the coded light": parked file.)

### from 5. Movement and acting
- [ ] EVERY move comes from the trained motion library (templates/motion_styles), picked by action + feeling + energy + character. Always comedy. ("we did train body movement character movement you didn't use any of them here")
- [ ] Bodies never pass through objects. Hands END ON what they touch. Things are held, carried or pushed; nothing floats or flies in. ("treasure flying in that's also wrong")
- [ ] EXPRESSIONS: every character starts with a calm normal face. The face changes ON the narration word to fit the action or scene, never before, then returns to calm. Idle = blinks only. ("the expression made at the same time of narration, not before")
- [ ] CHARACTER ACTING, MICRO-EXPRESSIONS, PERSONALITY-DRIVEN PHYSICAL COMEDY (CB 2026-11-13 02:03 Bangkok, pasted as a rule; his wording: rules/CB_WORDING_ARCHIVE.md): characters think, feel, anticipate and react, never perform a mechanical action. Every significant action carries ONE motivated behaviour detail from what the character thinks or does (tongue out of one mouth corner while concentrating, one eye squinted while aiming, lower lip bitten, one brow up when confused, head tilt, breath held on a delicate task), with facial asymmetry, eye-direction shifts, reaction delays, small wrist corrections and body language (tense shoulders, puffed chest). Each gag is an ACTING SEQUENCE with times, e.g. drilling: 0.0-1.0 s studies the target, head tilt, eyes narrow; 1.0-2.0 leans in, tongue slowly comes out; 2.0-3.5 drills, shoulders tense, brows furrowed; 3.5-4.2 drill jolts, he freezes, tongue still out; 4.2-5.0 slow glance to the camera, tongue back, embarrassed. Comedy comes from tiny unconscious habits, awkward pauses, overconfidence and unexpected reactions; no frozen faces, repeated gestures, random expressions or robotic moves. HOW IT FITS: the face starts calm and the big change lands ON the word (EXPRESSIONS); the detail plays DURING the action; once settled, DEAD STILL IN HOLDS wins; a head wobble with each expression change. The writer marks the detail per action, the animator acts it, the character-artist asks the lead for any missing face part (tongue-out mouth, one-eye squint, independent brows, lip bite). Section 12a builds on this rule.
- [ ] UNIVERSAL CHARACTER PERSONALITY, PSYCHOLOGY AND SOCIAL DYNAMICS (CB 2026-11-13 02:11 Bangkok, pasted as a rule; his 13 points in full: rules/CB_WORDING_ARCHIVE.md): every character has a distinct, persistent personality that shapes how they think, move, react and treat others. The 13 points: 1 a profile (temperament, confidence, competence, fears, motives, habits, quirks) kept across scenes; 2 personality-driven movement (calm expert deliberate, nervous beginner hesitates and overcorrects, arrogant one big gestures, sceptic restrained, arms crossed); 3 show, don't tell; 4 real skill is not shown confidence; 5 status and relationships shown by glances, spacing, interruptions; 6 contrast comedy (calm expert among panickers, confident fool beside a worried genius, the underestimated one who wins); 7 matching habits and micro-expressions; 8 supporting characters directed as carefully as the lead (true eye lines, delays, exchanged glances, based on what they see or know); 9 emotional continuity, no random changes between shots; 10 gags from traits and clashes; 11 subtlety, a small brow raise can beat a huge reaction; 12 each keeps posture, rhythm, gestures, reaction speed through the film; 13 status changes shown in performance. Never give all characters the same generic reactions. HOW WE RUN IT: the writer writes `episodes/<name>/CAST_PERSONALITY.md` before the shot table (per speaking or reacting character: the profile in short, posture, rhythm, 3-5 signature gestures, reaction speed, relationships and how they change); each picture-plan row says what each character in frame wants, knows and feels; the animator picks moves and timing from it; after a reaction settles DEAD STILL IN HOLDS applies; two characters reacting the same generic way, or a reaction that does not match what that character saw, fails.
- [ ] NO TELEPORT, NO MORPHING (CB 2026-11-11 on the roller coaster animatic: "many character just morph there. make rule no teleport morphing. sudden jump to a place"). A character or prop changes place ONLY by a move the viewer sees (walk, run, climb, ride, be carried, be pushed), or across a real cut or transition that the story has there. Never pop, fade, blend or slide to a new spot inside a running shot. A change of pose is ACTED through a move from the motion library (stand up, sit down, climb in, turn); never a blend from one unrelated pose into another. Things do not appear or vanish in view; they are brought in, or they are already there when the shot starts. Check: play the animatic and stop at every place change and every pose change; if you cannot name the move that got him there, it fails.

- [ ] LIGHT ON THE CHARACTERS (CB 2026-11-12: "include sunlight and light reflection, light source?"): every character is visibly lit by the scene's source (faces: colour only, see FACES). The side toward the sun, lamp, lantern or moon is brighter and takes that light's colour; a glint or rim on hair, hat, buckles and props from that source; hard shadow on the floor away from it. A card must never go dark because the light is behind it. Check one day and one night frame beside Rick before CB sees a set of shots.
- [ ] AIR LIFE AND WEATHER (CB 2026-11-12: "dust rain snow weather etc?"): every scene has air life that fits the place: dust motes in light beams, drifting haze, steam, smoke, insects or embers; weather where the story allows it (rain, snow, falling leaves, blowing sand) with surfaces to match (wet sheen, puddles, snow on roofs) and characters reacting to it. Indoors = dust in beams, smoke from burners; night = mist and moths at lanterns.
- [ ] LONG CLOTH MOVES WITH THE BODY (CB 2026-11-12 19:30 Bangkok "ok"): in every library move (pose m:<id> in films, rig_cast in tests) a long cloth (S.skirt) and a cape (S.behind) follow the legs the motion rig draws: upright the hem follows the legs; sitting it lies over the lap; kneeling, crouching, crawling or lying it wraps the legs and stops at the floor, never through a seat or the ground. No long bare legs beside a stiff robe. Cloth swings only during a move and settles within 8 to 12 frames; in a hold it is dead still. Keep it simple like Rick's robes. Check any new long outfit in walk, run, sit, kneel, jump, crawl and fall on the three body sizes before CB sees it.

- [ ] MOTION BLUR AND SPEED LINES (CB 2026-11-12 01:09 Bangkok: "no blur on character", speed lines "can have but make them look premium not like a kids cartoon"): characters are NEVER motion-blurred (a new sharp pose every frame, as Rick); fast moves get 1-2 smear frames instead. Motion blur is allowed on the world and fast props only (wheels, thrown things, the background in a whip). Speed lines are allowed again (this replaces the 2026-11-10 "no speed lines" line in the kit) but premium: thin, tapered, few, soft glow or air-streak in the scene's light colour, short-lived, following the real direction of travel; never thick black comic lines, stars or clip-art bursts.
- [ ] FULL BODY FORM, NEVER SQUASH: THE CAMERA COMES DOWN TO THE CHARACTER (CB 2026-11-12 10:44Z: "always show charcter the full form. neverr sqash. The full bodyform. need follow camera angle"; 11:05Z, rejecting the card-tilt method: "We study so many ricks clips. Please take the rules from there. Camera never stands at that angle need to pan down to the form of character"; measured on Rick's cart army, pink prison, grave bell, knight, drivers). Whenever a character is in frame, the camera stands at the character's height: between chest and eye level for talk and acts, or low near the ground looking up for power. Down-angle from camera to the character's chest at most 10 degrees. Characters always stand upright (card turns only around the vertical axis, Blender LOCKED_TRACK lock Z); never tip the card toward the lens. High or top-down views are only for objects and places with no character in frame. If a shot starts high on the set, the camera cranes/pans DOWN to the character's height before or as the character enters. Check: compute the down-angle to every character per shot before rendering. (Magic bell: anim_hook AN "crane" {cam, aim, end}. The TRACK_TO card tilt is withdrawn.)
- [ ] CHARACTER TRAITS MATCH THE STORY + CARTOON POWER VFX (CB 2026-11-12: "character eigenschaften match the story. use cartoon vfx or super power effects"): each character's look, outfit, build, props and way of moving say their role at first sight (clever judge = calm, tidy, sly half-smile; guilty thief = shifty eyes, sweat, hunched; brave guard = puffed chest). Feelings and acts are shown with cartoon effects in the story colours: sweat drops, anger steam, blush, a sparkle on a clever idea, a guilt aura or dark cloud, speed lines, shock lines, glowing eyes, stars after a hit, a power glow on the hero object. Every main beat gets at least one, on the narration word, built, popped and settled like the other VFX.

### from 6. Camera, transitions, effects, sound
- [ ] CAMERA: FLY, LAND, REST, FLY AGAIN (CB 2026-11-13 evening on the bomber armor animatic: "the camera movement is not what rick clips do", "too many cuts and just short camera fly, ricks clips have longer camere fly and stop then move. our move constant but in small moves only"; then "camere stops often. but i think it mean is mostly constaty moing not cuting frame if is not ncessary only when it change to another different location. also transition in object thats introduce a new scenen is is alos good to have"). ONE continuous camera that flies, lands, rests while the picture itself changes (acting, an effect, a board filling), and flies again, without cutting the frame. A cut or blend comes only when the story goes to a different location, and a transition THROUGH AN OBJECT that introduces the new scene is wanted there. The numbers (flying and rest shares, flight lengths, the first flight by 1 s, long flights attached to a moving thing or a set line) are section 11h, measured on all 26 of his films; they replace the one-film numbers of 2026-11-11 to 2026-11-13 ("moves 88-100 %", "rests 20-29 %"). This line replaces CAMERA MOVEMENT, ALWAYS and the camera bullets of RICK CAMERA AND SET BUILD.

### from 7. Before sending to CB (sign every line by looking, not by the gate report)
- [ ] UNIVERSAL CINEMATIC ANIMATION DIRECTOR, 15 PERMANENT STANDARDS (CB 2026-11-13 02:23 Bangkok: "about 80% of that master prompt is universal... Keep this as Claude's permanent master instruction"; full text in project files rules/CB_cinematic_master_2026-11-13.md). The crew works as a professional stylized 3D/2.5D studio and decides direction, camera, sets, acting, materials, light, physics, VFX and transitions from the story itself. The 15: personality, natural animation, facial acting, dialogue and lip sync, original gags, narrative world building, modelling and mechanics (primitives only for blocking), materials, cinematic lighting (motivated key, soft fill so shadows are never black, controlled rim, contact shadows, atmosphere, a grade for the story and time of day; no flat even brightness, over-saturated grass or flat skies), VFX, cinematography, physical consistency, continuity, stylized art direction (cast simple and clean, world rich), quality validation. Each has its full rule in sections 2-6; this line ties them together. Never force objects, effects or gags into a scene that does not need them. Never say an effect is built when the code only has a placeholder. (Its Blender tool line is parked with Blender.)
- [ ] SHOT-BY-SHOT VISUAL QA LOOP, 12 SCORES (CB 2026-11-13: "create the scene, render a preview, inspect the actual image, identify visible errors, and revise"): every shot is rendered and looked at, never judged from code. The storyboard-judge scores it 1-10 from visible evidence beside the reference in 12 categories: story accuracy, camera and framing, depth, environment richness, modeling detail, materials, lighting, character acting, physical grounding, VFX structure, colour grade, continuity. Any important category under 8 = revise. The judge runs as the tier says (11a2); the lead uses the same 12 categories in the self-review. Never claim an improvement without rendering and inspecting it, and say plainly what is still below the reference. These scores go on the PROOF PAGE.
- Premium detail: hero object, vehicle, structure, land and costume each checked at full size beside Rick's; lettering uses this story's words.
- [ ] 16-FRAME CHECK ON EVERY FINAL VIDEO (CB 2026-11-13 11:53 Bangkok "ok then add them", from a character-consistency course): pull 16 evenly spaced frames from the finished MP4 (and the animatic) into one contact sheet and look at each for melting or duplicated props, a colour or shape change on a character or prop, a background that jumps inside a shot, a character sunk into the ground or floating, and a missing signature detail. Any hit = fix and re-check before CB sees it. It sits beside the RANDOM-FRAME STILL CHECK.
- [ ] PROOF PAGE with every delivery: each panel beside its Rick frame, the judge's score, the measured numbers, and what is still below Rick. No proof page = unchecked work, do not send.
- [ ] Tell CB plainly what is not finished yet.

### from 8. Build fixes learned (magic bell 2026-11-11 and later; the Blender-only fixes are in rul
- [ ] Props that prove the story are built in 3D with their marks: the ink bell = glossy black body, four bronze handprints wiped out of the ink (palm + 4 fingers + thumb), drips at the lip.
- [ ] MECHANICS, BANNERS, EFFECTS (roller coaster round 2, CB's notes 2026-11-13 01:50 Bangkok: "summerize what you learn from this ... remember the camera movement"; full text project files episodes/roller-coaster/final/LESSONS_round2_2026-11-13.md): 1 cranks and handles turn with the fists ON the grip every frame: measure the fists per frame and drive the crank angle from that. 2 Banners hang still (stretched canvas on battens, no wind or folds); letters painted into the cloth material, never a see-through plane in front of a close character; nothing hangs in front of the words. 3 Mechanical motion follows the sound: a part that clicks 3 times moves in 3 steps with a small overshoot, never one smooth bend; when a part changes shape, hide every other version of it. 4 A person in a vehicle sits inside it: whole face in the windscreen, head under the roof; check the close shot. 5 Highlights on metal travel: they spread outward along the rail and slide, never sit still. 6 No effect freezes before the last frame: explosions keep growing and throwing bits to the end. 7 Wood reads as wood: grain along each part, knots, warm brown.

### from 9. LESSONS MERGED FROM THE SIDE NOTES (audit 2026-11-13; CB: "everything we learnd from th
- [ ] ONE VOICE, ALSO FOR QUOTED LINES (CB 2026-11-10, baboon film: "just tag different tone for speaker", "use same voice"). A character's quoted line is read by the same narrator voice with its own tone tag ([angry], [soft] ...). No second or third voice for characters, no cloned real-person voices. Reason: CB heard separate character voices and found them weird. Apply: the writer tags the quote line; the voice take is one speaker. Enforced by: writer check (one speaker id in the voice request).
- [ ] Footwear (CB 2026-11-10, Wrong Helmet cast): no shoes; if a story ever needs footwear it covers the whole foot.
- [ ] ONE CHARACTER FIRST (CB 2026-11-12 01:52 Bangkok: "show only one charcter template first"). A new outfit idea, body idea or finish is shown to CB on ONE standard character in the four views, and only after his OK rolled out to other forms and the cast. Reason: CB corrected each step live; a full sheet of a wrong idea wastes a round.
- [ ] (CB 2026-11-13 02:57 Bangkok: "but this depends on the story") The personality profile belongs to the FILM: it is written in that film's CAST_PERSONALITY.md under the character's ID. A profile stored in the preset is only an optional default. A costume for a new story becomes an approved variant of the same ID after CB has seen it.
- [ ] ANIMATICS ARE RENDERED AT FULL SIZE (CB 2026-11-11 17:03Z, roller coaster: "character need to be sharp everytime he is in the frame"). The soft characters came from a half-size animatic scaled up. Render every animatic CB sees with `render.mjs --animatic --scale 1` (1080x1920).
- [ ] THE HIGHLIGHT IS LIGHT ON THE NAMED OBJECT (CB 2026-11-10: "what about highlight vfx i didnt see anything?", then "too much cartoon highlight effects. like stars etc. that looks too cartoonish. it needs to look cool", then on the light-only version "Perfect now"). When a line names an object, that object's own surface glows in a flat saturated colour with a soft bloom for about a second, seen at first viewing. Metal gets ONE thin horizontal lens streak, never a cross (a cross reads as a star). No glow washed over a character; a face may change colour, only the face. Enforced by: film.json "highlights" (film.js: emissive tint + bloom, "flare": true).

### from 10. THE PROVEN BUILD METHOD (pin stretch test, CB 2026-11-14: "Yes, rebuild film". Proof: 
- Every act of every character is an episode move written for that act (a moves file in the stretch's cast folder, loaded as `m:../../<file>/<style>`), drawn new on every frame: `tween.ones` true, `face_frames` 0. Count before any render: plain kit poses 0, frozen moves 0.
- Things that go in, on or at something FLY there and HIT: flight with a streak, a one-frame hit, a mark, a quiver, dust, and the thing that is hit shudders. Nothing just appears.
- CLOSE-UPS ON WHAT THE VOICE NAMES, AS A SECONDARY RULE THAT MUST MATCH THE SCENE (CB 2026-11-14 on the joined armor film: "there are some like close up missing and frame by narration", "When you say hole, you need to show a hole", "Zoom to a hole"; then, correcting the lead who made it the top rule: "It's not primary, it's secondary. It needs to match the scene."). The scene comes first: its staging, its acting, the flow of the take. Where it fits that scene, the camera flies in and lands close on the thing the voice names, on the word, rests a beat and flies on; a named part may be highlighted with an effect. Never force a close-up on every noun and never chop a take into a string of inserts.

### from 11a2. QUALITY TIERS: STANDARD, PREMIUM, ULTRA (CB 2026-11-16: "can se set quality bar. lik
- a soft background behind big, close characters;
The lean pipeline took the light rounds out (they were done on still pictures), and nothing kept that guard. So the tiers now buy LOOK first, on the MOVING film, and add extra objects only where the camera is close. No tier uses Blender (CB: "no need bleder").

| | STANDARD | PREMIUM | ULTRA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tokens per finished minute | about 400 M (hard cap 450 M) | about 700 M (cap 780 M) | about 1 billion (cap 1.1 billion) |
| Edit rounds after the first full version (each = the lead's review of the whole film, then ONE batched fix round; CB's notes ride in these rounds) | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| LIGHT AND ATMOSPHERE (the biggest step between tiers) | the look pack's light per place: one key light, real shadows, the LOOK_BIBLE colours | a LIGHT PASS PER PLACE on the moving takes: warm key against cool shadow fill; haze in the depth (near clear, far soft); bloom and glow on lamps, windows and the hero's bright things; no vignette (only flashback or dream, section 3); depth of field that keeps the face sharp and softens the far background; light changing with the story clock. Checked beside the armor film and Rick frames of the same light | Premium's pass done PER SHOT: a key-light angle chosen for each framing; light streaks and shafts where the place has a source; rim light on the hero's silhouette (never a coloured rim on faces); a light change on every story beat; each power moment lighting the scene around it |
| COLOUR AND GRADE | 11c colours from day one, plus ONE grade over the whole film (the armor grade_final method) | plus the colour pass per place (set paint tuned to Rick's saturation, light kinds pushed further apart, measured with the colour-pass tools), then the grade | plus grade tuning per shot inside the film grade (match each cut, lift the hero, sink the edges) |
| DETAIL DENSITY (11i is the FLOOR for every tier: dressing step + gate, median edge density at least 0.14, no test frame under 0.08; Rick's 8 measured clips 0.10-0.18, median 0.14; a floor, not a score) | the 11i floor: every place dressed and passing the gate; reuse earlier sets and props where they pass | the 11i floor on every SHOT of the film (not only the test cameras), weak shots first; real-part hero props, story lettering, wear, near/mid/far layers | as Premium, with the near layer at Rick's densest (about 0.18 on close shots); every prop within 3 m of the lens built with real parts |

| Acting | library moves on every act, faces on the word | plus personal tics, and reactions from the people around | plus secondary motion on clothes, hair and props |
| Effects and gags | 3 power moments, 4 extreme gags | 4-5 power moments, 6 extreme gags, 1 POV, 1 impossible view | 5 power moments made for this story, 8 extreme gags, POV and impossible views wherever the plan allows, the last frame built as its own key image |

2. THE LAST LINE IS A PICTURE THAT PROVES THE MOCKED HERO RIGHT, readable with the sound off (the palace in rubble 34 M, the rails buckling under the train 29 M, the wave lifting the ship 16 M). Never end on a fact or a moral.

### from 11f. Camera and "power" effects as in Rick's latest three (CB 2026-11-16: "for camera and 
- IMPOSSIBLE VIEWS (CB 2026-11-16: "there is also one rule impossible view", then "Yes, add it"). One or two times per film, on a strong story moment, the camera sits where no real camera could be.
  - Rick's examples: inside the sheriff's eye, coming out as the driver's view; inside the old TV, looking out into the pink cell; straight down into the paint bucket as the red pours in; between the drilled holes of the cart board as the tubes slide in.
  - It must match the story: it shows the moment from the thing that matters most, the object, the body part or the hidden place.
  - Examples for our films:
    - from inside the Monopoly board, looking up as it is peeled open, with the silk unfolding over the lens;
    - from behind the mirror glass, looking out at the lady fixing her hair;
    - from inside the stuffed complaint box as the lid lifts;
    - from road level, as the stripes rush over the lens.
  - Enter and leave it with a camera move (a fly-through, a push or a dissolve on motion), never a hard cut. The frame edges show where we are (the inside of the board, the mirror's back, the box walls), so it reads at once.
  - The picture plan marks the row "IMPOSSIBLE VIEW", with where the camera is and why. Kid-safe: inside a body only in a cartoon way, never gory.

### from 11g. THE WORD MADE EXTREME: the universal visual gag (CB 2026-11-16, on two frames of Rick
- WHAT RICK DOES. When the voice says an amount, a size, a speed, a feeling or a figure of speech, the picture takes it LITERALLY and pushes it far past real, in the scene's own world, on that word. "A nice fat check" becomes a mountain of banknotes pouring over the whole front lawn while the fraudster grins beside his red car. "All that pain he's in" becomes him grinning in a hospital bed parked ON his own lawn, head bandaged, while the insurance man hands over a case of money. More from his films: "300 lb of tattoos" is a wall of a man; "[line from a reference film left out]" shows the milk cart; "Barbie's going to love it" (the pink cell); the giant flashing neon "HIT THIS TREE" arrow.

### from 11h. CAMERA MOVE LIBRARY, PICKED BY STORY JOB (CB 2026-11-16, decision card "Write the rul
2. The camera-director picks the move from the library menu for that tag and writes "row -> Mxx, attached to (thing, line or object), reason" in CAMERA_NOTE.md. Rows with the same tag in one place share ONE move. No move without a reason; an orbit (M16) only at a story peak.
5. Camera-safe inside every move: character height within 10 degrees down when a face is in frame, never pass behind a figure, views from apply_looks; run frame_checks and validate.mjs at 0/25/50/75/100 % of each flight, not only on rests.
6. Tool gaps until film_plan.py is updated: follow works for characters only (props, effects and set lines need pass-points every 0.5 s); curves need pass-point stations (hold 0); travel over 3 s must be set by hand; the gate "word stations not at rest on their word" is to be removed (it forces a stop per noun).
10. CAMERA DON'TS: WHAT MUST NEVER HAPPEN (CB 2026-11-16: "should we have what should not happend? also added to it"; from his points 7, 11 and 12 and from his past rejections). Any one of these in a version = not ready for CB.
   - A character teleports or morphs to a new place or pose; places change only by a seen move or a real cut (section 5 NO TELEPORT, NO MORPHING).
   - The camera turns, moves, squashes or re-poses a character, or changes an approved look, size, colour or face. The camera only looks at the one world (11d2, camsafe, point 12).
   - An edge-on or thin card, a flattened face, a stretched or distorted body, the wrong view for the angle, a back view of the subject, an eyeline that misses its target, feet off the ground, a hand that does not touch its prop (camsafe validate.mjs, frame_checks seat, slide and prop_in_hand).
   - A cut or a new framing for every sentence or every noun; a hard cut inside one place; more than 1 hard cut per 10 s (6b, 11f).
   - A camera that hops in short 0.3-0.5 s moves between many stations, or stops dead and freezes; a rest is always alive (M00).
   - A decorative orbit, a random zoom or push, a random shake, a move with no story job; shake only on a hit, 3-8 frames, decaying, with its sound (11f).
   - A jerky, whipped or linear move: no ease, a sudden direction flip, more than about 40 px per frame (60 only for the one planned crash zoom) (11f).
   - Tilt (roll) while resting; roll only inside a move and level on landing.
   - A long slow fade, or a transition with no motion; place changes are a flight, a dissolve on motion, a match or a fly-through (6, 6b, 11f).
   - A wide where a close-up must explain an object or an action; the subject blocked, cropped by accident, under the caption band, or lost in empty space (section 6).
   - The camera passing behind a figure, or below 10 degrees down on a face at character height when it is close (camsafe FACE_BEHIND, STEEP, LOW).
   - The screen direction, object positions or blocking flipping between shots of the same moment (11d2).
   - Camera direction judged or approved from stills alone.



### from 11i. THE WORLD AT RICK'S DETAIL: a measured detail gate and a dressing step, standard for 
- THE DRESSING STEP (part of the set round, from the first day; never a repaint later): every place gets a dressing pass that fills the mid-ground with this story's own things: full-foliage trees and bushes (no bare sticks unless the story is winter), textured grass, kerbs and gutters, street furniture (benches, bins, hydrants, poles, signs with real faces), parked and moving vehicles with real parts, background people, facade detail (balconies, awnings, storefronts, ledges, roof clutter, lit and unlit windows varied), surface wear (patches, stains, puddles, cracks, leaves). A NAMED PROP LIST PER SET (CB 2026-11-17: "what you can learn fromhere to make our video better", then "yes can add all"; source: the "Miner Who Fed Ghosts" prompt, project files rules/miner_prompt_2026-11-17.md): `PROPS.md` (11a 1b check 2) has one section per set naming every prop and dressing item that set holds, and WEAR AND IMPERFECTIONS ON EVERYTHING: cracks, chips, knots, rust and flaking paint, wax drips, soot, damp and mineral stains, moss, mud, frayed edges, placed where they would really gather; nothing clean, nothing that repeats like a pattern. Also small props on every table and shelf indoors, and two air layers. Each object real-size and from this place and era; nothing generic (Hard Rule No. 2). The dressing never sits between the camera and a face and never blocks a planned camera path (check the frame checks after dressing).
